newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Tearful Bosnian voters dream of going home.
newsitem.headline: Tearful Bosnian voters dream of going home.

text.p: Bosnians battered by war voted in elections on Saturday designed to anchor a new peace, many of them refugees whose eyes welled with tears as they voiced dreams of returning to their old homes.

Every refugee -- whether they flocked to the polls in the capital Sarajevo or boarded buses for a NATO-guarded journey to vote in former home towns -- could remember the day they were driven into exile.
Moslem refugees driven out by separatist Serbs all hoped the elections mandated by the 1995 Dayton peace treaty would lead to Bosnia's reunification, to bring them finally home.

Native Sarajevans, who voted in the shadow of hills from which Serbs besieged the capital for 43 months, were more sceptical, trusting Dayton's unity agenda to stay on track only if NATO peace troops stayed indefinitely.

"Dayton said we should already have been back in our homes for Election Day, but we aren't. Still we hope the elections will be a big step for the Dayton process," said Akif Memisevic, 65, expelled with his wife Esrefa from Pale in 1992.
Scores of Moslem refugees gathered in Sarajevo's Ottoman mediaeval quarter to board buses for polling places in Serb-controlled eastern Bosnia.
"I was driven off my farm near Sokolac on July 27, 1992 and hid in the woods for a week with my wife before escaping to free (Bosnian government) territory," recalled Meho Dzindo.
"I consider these elections a historic moment, the way to making Bosnia whole and democratic again," he said.
"I've met my old Serb neighbours at the marketplace on the boundary line near here and they say they look forward to me coming back because they can't stand living only among Serb refugees any more."
Munir and Azamina Pijalovic, a Sarajevo couple, hoped the elections would solidify a tenuous peace and bring back jobs and hope for young people.
Azamina, her eyes watering, produced photographs of her daughters in an idyllic country meadow and said: "We pray to God for a better future from these elections to bring our daughters home."
Some Moslem voters wanted all of Bosnia back again, but not necessarily with the Serbs around.

Ferida Ribic, 52, cast her ballot at the base of Trebevic mountain where her son was killed by Serbs in battle in 1993. "If Serbs want to live with us again, ok. But I won't consort with them because they took away my boy."

Most people voting in Sarajevo said they had chosen the Moslem national party of Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic, which wants to restore a united Bosnia in contrast with the ruling parties in separatist Serb and Croat regions.
Izetbegovic voted in the same street where separatist Serb leader Radovan Karadzic once lived. The president abandoned his flat on the street after Serb artillery targeted it in 1992.
"We are voting for a Bosnia where nobody will be persecuted because of his religion, nation or political orientation," the 71-year-old president told reporters.
Kresimir Zubak, Croat president of Bosnia's federation with Moslems, voted as a refugee near Doboj in the Serb-held north.
"These elections are very important for fostering a long- lasting peace and rebuilding confidence between peoples to renew life and work," Zubak said.
Acting Bosnian Serb president Biljana Plavsic, who took over from Karadzic when he was forced to step down as an indicted war criminal, voted in Banja Luka in the north.
"I hope the elections on the whole territory of the Bosnian Serb Republic will pass in a democratic atmosphere and that people will vote for the Bosnian Serb Republic," she said.
Refugees heading for ballot centres in Serb territory backed SDA exile candidates for both the new Bosnia-wide parliament and the regional Serb assembly.
But they could not vote for Moslem and Croat candidates for the Bosnian collective presidency as the presidential ballot in Serb territory was reserved for Serbs.
Unable to vote for Izetbegovic, Moslem refugees bound for polling centres on Serb terrain said their presidential choice would probably be Mladen Ivanic, a moderate Serb.

"I will vote for progressive candidates, maybe Ivanic," said Hasena Mesidzic, kicked out of Visegrad in 1992. "It's not clear to me what the election outcome will be but I can only hope for the country coming together again gradually."
